summary: Help 7–9 year-olds understand animal migration as a regular round-trip journey (usually seasonal and yearly; for salmon a once-in-a-lifetime round trip, for monarchs one spread over several generations) driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season — not any one-off long movement. Learners map real routes for several species (Arctic tern, monarch, wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon), link each leg of a journey to a season and its reason, and explore how animals navigate using real cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell). The centrepiece is a season-driven map the learner runs, so migration appears as a timed response to a changing habitat; map-reveal, sorting, and recall activities support and check the same ideas.
misconceptions: 'Any long journey is migration' — migration is regular, seasonal, and a round trip, not a one-off move.
'Only birds migrate' — mammals (whales, wildebeest), fish (salmon), insects (monarchs) and others migrate too.
'Animals migrate because they get bored/cold and just leave' — the drivers are specific: food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season.
'The same individual butterfly flies all the way to Mexico and back' — the monarch round trip spans multiple generations.
'Animals have no way to navigate — they just know' — they use real cues: sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell.

activities.title: Run a season-driven migration map
steps: Pick a migrant (e.g. swallow, Arctic tern, wildebeest) and watch where it starts on a world map.

Turn a calendar/season dial and observe the 'good' habitat move across the map — for example grass greening in a summer feeding region, or breeding waters warming in a breeding region — while the animal's food/breeding meter responds. (Which direction is 'good' depends on the species: swallows breed in the northern summer, humpback whales breed in warm tropical waters.)
Move the animal to follow the shifting habitat, discovering that staying put makes the food or breeding meter drop.
Advance through a full year so the animal travels out AND back, matching each leg to a season and its reason (feed / breed / escape harsh season).
For the monarch route, watch a generation counter show that the animal that sets out is often not the one that arrives.
activities.insight: Migration is a regular, seasonal, there-and-back journey that an animal makes because the habitat offering food or breeding sites shifts with the seasons — it is purposeful, not aimless wandering, and for monarchs the round trip spans multiple generations.

activities.title: Steer by the animal's navigation cues
steps: Take control of a migrant and try to stay on its route, using the animal's real cues: the sun's position, the stars, Earth's magnetic field, coastal landmarks, or (for salmon) the smell of its home river.
Try the cues one at a time as a game, then notice that real animals often use several cues together to stay on course.
Match each cue to an animal that famously uses it (e.g. salmon and home-river smell).
activities.insight: Animals do not 'just know' the way — they use real, nameable cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell), often several together, to navigate long journeys.

activities.title: Map and label real migration routes
steps: On a world map, tap or trace the route of at least three migrants out and back.
For each, read or reveal why it goes (following food, reaching breeding grounds, escaping winter/dry season) and roughly how far.

Pair a summer feeding ground with a winter breeding ground for a migrant that fits this pattern (e.g. humpback whale: polar summer feeding, tropical winter breeding) to see the before/after habitat contrast — swallows do the reverse, breeding in the northern summer.
activities.insight: Real migrants span many animal groups — birds (Arctic tern, swallow), mammals (whale, wildebeest), fish (salmon), insects (monarch) — and each route has a destination and a reason, making the scale and purpose of the journeys concrete.

activities.title: The return-trip puzzle (talk and reason)
steps: Consider: every autumn swallows fly thousands of miles from Britain to Africa, then fly all the way back in spring — why not just stay in warm Africa all year? Why make the journey twice?
State a reason the swallows come BACK, not just why they leave.
Decide and explain: is a hedgehog that sleeps all winter migrating? Sort several animals into 'migrates' vs 'hibernates'.
Name another animal that migrates and say what it is travelling towards.

Answer a what-if: if there were plenty of insects in Britain all winter, would the swallows still leave? (Discuss both sides: the urge to leave is inherited and triggered by cues like shortening days, so many might still go, but over many generations food availability shapes where and whether a species migrates.)
activities.insight: Migration follows food and breeding across the seasons, not just warmth — which is why there is a return leg. It is distinct from hibernation (stay put and sleep) and is an inherited, instinctive pattern triggered by cues like shortening daylight, not a human-like planned choice.

activities.title: Check the definition: match, sequence, define
steps: Match each migrant to its route and its driver (food / breeding / escaping a harsh season).
Put the legs of one journey in the correct order by season.
Choose the statement that correctly defines migration and separate it from a one-off wandering move.
Identify the error in statements like 'the same butterfly flies all the way to Mexico and back' or 'only birds migrate'.
activities.insight: Migration is defined by being regular, seasonal, and a round trip — and learners can apply that definition to tell true migration from one-off movement and to catch common mistakes.

checkQuestion: Every autumn, swallows fly thousands of miles from Britain all the way to Africa — and then fly the whole way back again in spring. Why don't they just stay in warm Africa all year? Why make the journey twice?
checkAnswer: They return because migration follows food and breeding, not just warmth. In the northern spring and summer there are huge numbers of insects to eat, long daylight, and good, safe places to nest and raise young; by autumn that food runs out, so they travel back to Africa where food is plentiful over winter. Each place gives them what they need at that time of year, so the round trip is worth it — it's about food and raising young, not simply escaping the cold.
